Newborn Care

Vitamin C for babies: food, milk and supplements

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Vitamin C helps the body make connective tissue, supports normal immune function and improves absorption of iron from plant foods. Babies need it as part of their overall nutrition. For most families, the starting point is appropriate milk feeding, followed by varied complementary foods: not a high-dose vitamin C product.

How much does a baby need?

The US dietary reference values use an adequate intake of 40 milligrams a day from birth through six months and 50 milligrams from seven through twelve months. These are estimates of total intake from all sources, based on the available nutrition evidence.

They are not instructions to give that amount as drops in addition to milk and food. Parents do not need to calculate the vitamin C content of every feed. Growth, feeding history, food variety and any medical needs are more useful topics to discuss with your child's clinician.

Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is water-soluble and must come from the diet because the body cannot make it. It helps form collagen, a structural protein in skin and other tissues, and acts as an antioxidant. Antioxidants help limit damage from reactive molecules produced during normal metabolism; vitamin C is one of several nutrients with this role.

Milk is an important source in the early months

Breast milk provides vitamin C, and commercial infant formula is fortified with it. Prepare formula exactly as directed; do not add vitamin powders, extra scoops or juice to increase its nutritional value.

If your baby was born prematurely, has a medical condition or has difficulty feeding or absorbing nutrients, the feeding plan may be different. Follow the neonatal or paediatric team's advice rather than applying general guidance about a healthy term baby.

Breastfeeding parents also need enough vitamin C. The US recommended intake for a lactating adult aged 19 or older is 120 milligrams a day, while the value for a breastfeeding adolescent is 115 milligrams. These are total dietary targets, not a routine recommendation for megadose supplements.

Supplement recommendations differ between countries

A separate vitamin C supplement is not routinely needed for many healthy babies receiving appropriate milk and food. However, this should not be turned into a rule that infant vitamin drops are always unnecessary.

UK guidance recommends daily vitamins A, C and D from six months to five years, with an exception for babies drinking more than 500 millilitres of infant formula a day because it is already fortified. Breastfed babies are included in the six-month recommendation; they are not excluded.

Vitamin D has its own guidance. For example, UK advice recommends it from birth for breastfed babies, regardless of the parent's vitamin D supplement use. Other countries use different policies and formula-volume thresholds. Ask your local child-health professional which age-appropriate product, if any, your baby needs.

Offer food sources when your baby is ready for solids

Around six months, when developmentally ready, a baby can begin complementary foods while continuing breast milk or formula. Suitable vitamin C sources include broccoli, peppers, kiwi, strawberries and other fruit and vegetables, prepared in a form your baby can manage.

Cook firm vegetables until soft, remove pits and other hard parts, and mash or cut foods appropriately. Avoid whole round berries and hard chunks. Seat your baby upright and supervise throughout eating. A food being rich in a vitamin does not make its original shape safe.

You can pair a vitamin C food with an iron-rich food, such as soft lentils or fortified infant cereal. Offer small portions and allow repeated, relaxed exposure to new flavours. There is no need to pressure your baby to finish a calculated percentage of a daily target.

Fruit juice is not needed as a vitamin supplement, and babies younger than twelve months should not routinely have it. Appropriately prepared whole fruit offers a better way to introduce the food alongside the rest of the diet.

Other options include soft papaya and suitably prepared mandarin flesh. Small example portions might be about 23 grams of red pepper, 41 grams of strawberries, 44 grams of kiwi, 24 grams of mandarin or cooked broccoli, or 57 grams of papaya. These are illustrations of food variety, not portions a baby must finish. Vitamin content varies with the food and preparation, and the percentage of a daily reference value changes with age; a single percentage is not a feeding target.

More is not necessarily better

High doses of vitamin C can cause diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal discomfort. The absence of an established upper intake limit for infants reflects insufficient evidence, not proof that any amount is safe. Adult chewables, effervescent tablets and concentrated powders are not appropriate substitutes for infant products.

Check all supplement labels with a pharmacist or clinician. Combining drops with a multivitamin or another product can duplicate nutrients, including vitamins A and D. Use the measuring device supplied with the recommended product and keep supplements out of children's reach.

Vitamin C supports normal immune function, but extra doses are not a reliable way to prevent your baby catching infections. Do not replace feeding advice, vaccination or medical assessment with an immunity supplement.

Large supplemental doses may increase urinary oxalate and can be a concern in people prone to kidney stones or with kidney disease. This does not mean ordinary vitamin C foods cause stones in a healthy baby. Ask the treating clinician before adding supplements when kidney health is an issue.

When to ask for a nutrition review

Severe vitamin C deficiency can cause scurvy, but it is uncommon in a baby with adequate nutrition. A very restricted diet, poor intake or a condition affecting absorption may increase concern.

Poor growth, persistent feeding difficulty, unusual bruising or bleeding, or marked tiredness needs medical assessment. These symptoms have many possible causes; do not diagnose a vitamin deficiency yourself. A clinician can review the diet and decide whether tests or a prescribed supplement are appropriate.

Conditions causing a very restricted diet, malabsorption or major illness, including some cancer treatments, can increase concern. A neurodevelopmental diagnosis alone does not prove deficiency; the actual feeding pattern matters. Scurvy can cause sore or bleeding gums, poor wound healing, tiredness, irritability and poor appetite. Untreated severe deficiency can become serious, so assessment is better than guessing a supplement dose.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Dietary reference values describe total intake, while infant supplement policy depends on age, feeding and country.

NHS recommends age-appropriate A, C and D drops from six months for eligible children and vitamin D from birth for breastfed babies; high-dose vitamin C is not a substitute.

How BeMama can help

Use milk feeding and a varied, safely prepared complementary diet as the foundation, with local advice on the exact vitamin product.

When to seek help

Poor growth, unusual bleeding or persistent feeding difficulty needs assessment; do not use adult supplements or diagnose scurvy from symptoms alone.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Infant intake values refer to milk, food and supplements combined.
  • Breast milk and fortified formula provide vitamin C.
  • Follow local infant-vitamin guidance; UK advice includes A, C and D from six months for eligible babies.
  • Avoid adult products and high doses, and prepare vitamin-rich foods safely.

Frequently asked questions

Does 40 milligrams mean I should give 40 milligrams of drops?

No. It is a reference value for total intake, not an extra dose on top of feeding.

Are breastfed babies excluded from the UK six-month vitamin recommendation?

No. The advice includes breastfed babies. The formula-volume exception is a separate consideration.

Should I give orange juice for vitamin C?

Not routinely before twelve months. Milk and suitable complementary foods can provide vitamin C without using juice as a supplement.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
